lesson.title: Charging: the charger holds volts per cell

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is sulphate growing on the negative plate below the float band and the positive grid thinning above it, when you drag the set point in volts per cell.

interactive.whatAmILookingAt: On the left is a charger. It is drawn as a box that holds a set voltage and limits its current. Its two leads feed a string of lead-acid cells. A cell stepper sets how many: 6, 12, 24 or 55. One cell is drawn cut open, as in lesson 1. It has a lead dioxide positive plate, a lead negative plate and acid between them. Above sits a set-point slider in volts per cell, from 2.10 to 2.60. It is marked in bands. Float runs from 2.23 to 2.27, and boost from 2.33 to 2.40. A red gassing line sits at 2.40, and equalise at 2.50. The charger's volts are the set point times the number of cells. Below runs a trace of an example 100 Ah battery charged from flat, with a time scrubber. It draws volts per cell and current together against time. In the bulk stage the charger holds the current at an example 10 A. The volts per cell climb as the cell fills. In the topping stage the charger holds the volts at an example charge setting of 2.35. Charge settings range from 2.30 to 2.45 a cell, and this one sits inside that range. The current tails off to 3 to 5 A, which is 3 to 5 per cent of 100 Ah. In the float stage the volts drop to 2.25 a cell. A small current then makes up the cell's self-discharge. The trace is a sketch. Two meters show what months at the set point do to the plates. They show the direction only. Below the float band, a sulphate layer grows on the negative plate. Above it, the positive grid thins. Past 2.40, bubbles rise from both plates and a water gauge falls. A temperature slider runs from 15 to 35 °C. It moves the float figure by 3 mV a cell for each degree away from 25 °C. Warmer moves it down, and colder moves it up. On a phone the three readouts wrap onto a second line, and no word splits. Each show screen has under about 90 words. It ends on what its finished picture shows, so it reads well without the controls. Screen by screen. 1 asks what the charger reads when a bank of 12 cells floats at 2.25 V a cell. The choices are 27 V, 25.2 V or 2.25 V. The right pick says 'That's it: 12 × 2.25 = 27.00 V.' Hint for 25.2 V: that is 12 × 2.1 V, the rested voltage. A charger must sit above it to push current in. Hint for 2.25 V: that is one cell, and cells in series add. 2 plays a charge from flat. The current holds at 10 A while the volts per cell climb. The volts reach 2.35, inside the boost band, and hold, and the current tails off. Then the volts drop to 2.25 for float, and a small current flows. It ends on float. 3 says the topping current on the 100 Ah battery has fallen from 10 A. It now holds at 4 A. The screen asks whether the battery is charged. First choice: yes, because 4 A is 4 per cent of 100 Ah. Second: no, because full means 0 A. Third: no, because the current should still be 10 A. Hint for 0 A: a full cell held at the charge setting never quite reaches 0 A, so compare 4 A with the 100 Ah. Hint for 10 A: a steady 10 A is the bulk stage. A falling current means the cell is filling. 4 steps the cell count at a float of 2.23 V a cell. Six cells need 13.38 V, 12 need 26.76 V and 24 need 53.52 V. It ends on 24 cells at 53.52 V. 5 asks what to set the charger to for 55 cells at 2.23 V a cell. The choices are 122.65 V, 115.50 V or 110.00 V. Hint for 115.50 V: that is 55 × 2.1 V, the rested voltage. Almost no current would flow in. Hint for 110.00 V: that is the nominal 2 V a cell. It is below a charged battery's own voltage, so the charger would put nothing into it. 6 moves the set point from 2.25 down to 2.15. The sulphate meter on the negative plate climbs. Then the set point moves up to 2.45. The sulphate meter stops, and the grid meter on the positive plate climbs. Bubbles rise and the water gauge falls. It ends back at 2.25, with both meters still. 7 says the float has been raised from 2.25 to 2.35 V a cell to keep the bank fuller. It asks what a year of that does. First choice: the positive grid corrodes faster and the cells run warmer. Second: more ampere-hours in store. Third: nothing, because a full cell takes no more charge. Hint for more ampere-hours: a full cell is full. The extra volts push current it cannot store. Hint for nothing: at 2.35 a full cell still takes current, so where can that current go? 8 says a boost is a spell above float that refills the cells faster, and the topping stage at 2.35 was one. It sets the set point to 2.38 after a discharge, in the boost band. The current is limited, and the scrubber reaches full sooner. At full the charger drops back to float. Then it sets 2.50 to equalise, and bubbles rise from every cell. It ends on float. 9 says Friday's discharge was recharged on boost at 2.40 V a cell. On Monday the charger is still on boost. It asks what the weekend has done. First choice: extra grid corrosion and water lost as gas. Second: extra capacity from charging past full. Third: nothing, because a full battery takes no current. Hint for extra capacity: boost is for recharging. Once the battery is full, the extra current goes to heat, gas and corrosion. Hint for nothing: held at 2.40, a full cell keeps taking current. 10 sets 24 cells and moves the temperature from 25 to 35 °C. The float falls from 2.25 to 2.22 V a cell. The charger falls from 54.00 to 53.28 V. It ends at 35 °C. 11 asks what float to set for cells at 15 °C. They float at 2.25 V a cell at 25 °C, and the setting moves 3 mV a cell for each degree away from 25 °C. The choices are 2.28 V, 2.22 V or 2.25 V. Hint for 2.22 V: that is the warm correction, and colder raises the setting. Hint for 2.25 V: the cells are 10 degrees below 25 °C, so the setting moves. 12, 13 and 14 mix the ideas. 12 says a 24-cell charger has sat at 51.60 V for a year. It asks what that has done. First choice: sulphate building on the negative plates. Second: corrosion of the positive grid. Third: nothing, because 2.15 V a cell is above the rested 2.1 V. Hint for corrosion: 51.60 ÷ 24 is 2.15 V a cell, below the float band. So the cells are undercharged. Hint for nothing: 2.15 V a cell is below the float band, so the cells are not kept full. 13 says the specific gravities of a 24-cell battery have drifted apart after months on float. It asks what the battery needs. First choice: an equalise at 2.50 V a cell, 60.00 V, then back to float. Second: the float raised to 60.00 V for good. Third: boost at 2.40 V a cell, 57.60 V, left on. Hint for float raised for good: equalise is a deliberate overcharge, safe only for a while. Hint for boost left on: boost recharges, then must go back to float. 14 draws a simple charging circuit. A DC supply feeds the battery positive to positive, through a resistor and an ammeter. The battery gave out 50 Ah. It asks how many ampere-hours the supply must put back. The choices are 60 Ah, 50 Ah or 42 Ah. Two bars show 50 Ah taken out and the ampere-hours put back. On a right answer the second bar fills to 60 Ah, and a line says about 83 per cent comes back. Hint for 50 Ah: some of the charge splits water into gas instead of filling the plates. Hint for 42 Ah: that is less than came out.
interactive.ignores: The charge is sped up from hours to seconds. The trace is a smooth sketch. The meters show only which way sulphate and corrosion go, not how fast. Every cell is drawn the same, and they share the charger's volts equally. Real cells differ a little, and in a string that matters. The charger's insides are left out, with its ripple and its own current limit on boost. The cell is a flooded one. A sealed cell has its own, tighter figures. The float band's bottom edge, 2.23 V, is a 20 °C figure, while its top and the temperature rule work from 25 °C.

explain.text:
A charger refills a lead-acid battery by holding a set voltage on every cell. It works in three stages: bulk, topping and float. The setting per cell sits in a narrow band. Set it a little too low, and sulphate builds on the negative plate. Set it too high, and the positive grid corrodes.

Charging runs lesson 1's reaction backwards. The sulphate on both plates turns back into lead and lead dioxide. The acid returns to the liquid. In the bulk stage the charger holds its current steady. The volts per cell climb as the cell fills. When they reach the charge setting, the charger holds the volts instead. That is the topping stage. Now the current falls by itself, because the cell is saturating. With less sulphate left to turn back, the same volts push less current in. A cell counts as full when the current has fallen to 3 to 5 per cent of its Ah rating.[^7] On a 100 Ah battery, that is 3 to 5 A. Then the charger drops to the [[float charge]]. A large stationary battery floats at about 2.25 V a cell at 25 °C.[^2] That is enough above its rested 2.1 V to push a small current. This small current makes up the cell's self-discharge. Holding the volts is what lets the current fall away. A fixed current would keep flowing into a full battery. A full cell cannot store that current, so it turns into heat and gas.

Not all the charge comes back out. Some of it splits water into gas instead of filling the plates. So you put back about 1.2 times the ampere-hours taken out. Put the other way, about 83 per cent of the ampere-hours come back. The simplest charger is a DC supply set above the battery's voltage. Join positive to positive and negative to negative, so the supply pushes current into the battery. A resistor in series limits the current, and an ammeter in series shows it.

Each cell's band comes from its own chemistry, and cells in series add their volts. So you set one cell's figure and multiply by the cells. The charger's volts are the float volts per cell times the number of cells. A typical vented cell floats at 2.23 V a cell at 20 °C. So 24 cells need 2.23 × 24 = 53.52 V. The band is narrow because both sides do harm. Held too low, the cells never quite get back to full. The sulphate left on the negative plate builds up. Held too high, current keeps flowing into a full cell. Picture it this way. With little sulphate left to convert, that current works on the lead grid that holds the positive plate together. The grid corrodes. Past 2.40 V a cell the cells also gas freely. So higher is not better. It swaps one kind of damage for another.

Two settings sit above float on purpose, for a while. A [[boost charge]] is a spell above float that refills the cells faster after a discharge. It typically runs at 2.33 to 2.40 V a cell, so the topping stage of a normal charge is usually a boost. It must go back to float once the battery is full. An [[equalising charge]] is a deliberate overcharge, typically at 2.50 V a cell.[^5] It clears built-up sulphate and brings the cells level. Temperature moves the band too. Picture it this way: a warm cell reacts more readily, so the same volts push more current in. So a warm cell needs a lower setting. A typical correction is 3 mV a cell off for each degree above 25 °C, and 3 mV a cell on for each degree below.[^6] So a 2.25 V float becomes 2.22 V at 35 °C. Some makers correct only outside 10 to 30 °C. So follow the battery's own maker. These figures are for flooded cells. Sealed cells tolerate overcharge less and have their own figures. **A charger holds a set voltage per cell, multiplied by the number of cells. That setting lives in a narrow band: too low sulphates the negative plate, and too high corrodes the positive grid.**

analogy.text: Think of tyre pressure. The maker gives one figure per tyre, and you set each tyre to it. Too soft, and the shoulders wear and the tyre runs hot. Too hard, and the centre wears and grip falls. Neither side is safe. So 'a bit more to be sure' does harm. You also check the pressure cold, because heat raises the reading. A charger's set point works the same way: one figure per cell, harm on both sides, corrected for temperature.
analogy.breaks: A tyre is pumped up now and then, and holds its pressure in between. A charger's volts push a current all the time. The harm comes from that current, through the reactions at the plates. The cell's band is also far narrower: a few hundredths of a volt in about 2.25.

practice.text:
Use this to set or check a charger on a lead-acid battery.

- Before a boost or an equalise, check the battery room's ventilation works. Gas climbs steeply from about 2.40 V a cell, and even a boost near full makes a little.
- Find the maker's float figure in volts per cell, and the temperature it is quoted at.
- Count the cells in series. A 12 V block holds six.
- Multiply: charger volts = volts per cell × number of cells.
- Correct for the battery's temperature by the maker's rule. Warmer means a lower setting.
- After a discharge, expect to put back about 1.2 times the ampere-hours taken out.
- After a boost or an equalise, check the charger has gone back to float.

**Rule of thumb:** divide the charger's reading by the number of cells. On float it should land in the maker's band. For flooded cells near room temperature, that is around 2.23 to 2.27 V a cell.

**Worked example:** A battery of 55 vented cells floats at 2.23 V a cell at 20 °C. Its maker leaves the setting alone from 10 to 30 °C. Above 30 °C, it takes off 0.003 V a cell for each degree over. The cells run at 35 °C, which is 5 degrees over. So the float is 2.23 − 0.015 = 2.215 V a cell. Set the charger to 2.215 × 55 = 121.8 V.

**Common mistakes**
- Setting the charger to the nominal or rested voltage times the cells.
- Raising the float to keep the battery fuller.
- Leaving a boost or an equalise running.
- Getting the temperature sign backwards: warmer needs less.
- Using one maker's figures on another maker's battery.

sources.quote: The recommended float / charge voltage is 2.23 V/cell remove per cell at 20°C (68°F) depending on the specific type (see table 5). The charger voltage amounts to Uflo per cell x no. of cells (tolerance ± 1 %).

sources.title: Bu 403 Charging Lead Acid — Battery University
sources.quote: The recommended float voltage of most flooded lead acid batteries is 2.25V to 2.27V/cell. Large stationary batteries at 25°C (77°F) typically float at 2.25V/cell.

sources.quote: To reduce the recharge time the battery may be recharged at 2.33 – 2.40 V/cell with a current limited to 4 x I10. Boost charging must be switched to float charging when the fully charged state is reached.

sources.title: Flooded Stationary Lead Acid Batteries IOM — EnerSys
sources.quote: After reaching the gassing voltage of 2.40 V/c a current limit of 2.5 to 5 A/100 Ah is recommended

sources.title: BU-404: What is Equalizing Charge? - Battery University
sources.quote: Applying a periodic equalizing charge brings all cells to similar levels by increasing the voltage to 2.50V/cell, or 10 percent higher than the recommended charge voltage.

sources.title: Bu 403 Charging Lead Acid — Battery University
sources.quote: the charge voltage should be reduced by 3mV per cell for every degree above 25°C and increased by 3mV per cell for every degree below 25°C.

sources.title: Bu 403 Charging Lead Acid — Battery University
sources.quote: full charge is reached when the current decreases to 3–5 percent of the Ah rating.

sources.title: Bu 403 Charging Lead Acid — Battery University
sources.quote: The correct setting of the charge voltage limit is critical and ranges from 2.30V to 2.45V per cell.

sources.title: Battery University | BU-303: Confusion with Voltages
sources.quote: The nominal voltage of lead acid is 2 volts per cell, however when measuring the open circuit voltage, the OCV of a charged and rested battery should be 2.1V/cell.

sources.title: Flooded Stationary Lead Acid Batteries IOM — EnerSys
sources.quote: If the average battery temperature exceeds the recommended operating temperature range of +10°C (50°F) to +30°C (86°F), the float charge voltage shall be reduced by (Tcell - 30) x 0.003V/ cell when the temperature exceeds +30°C (86°F)

sources.quote: Some batteries are designed for single-use applications and cannot be recharged (primary cells), while others are based on conveniently reversible cell reactions that allow recharging by an external power source (secondary cells).

checks.label: The charger voltage is the float volts per cell times the number of cells: at 2.23 V a cell, 6 cells need 13.38 V, 12 need 26.76 V, 24 need 53.52 V and 55 need 122.65 V
Large stationary batteries at 25 °C typically float at 2.25 V a cell: the charge ends on float at 2.25 V a cell, and 12 cells there need 27.00 V
The charge voltage drops 3 mV a cell for every degree above 25 °C and rises 3 mV for every degree below: 2.25 V becomes 2.22 V at 35 °C and 2.28 V at 15 °C, and 24 cells go from 54.00 V to 53.28 V
Full charge is reached when the current falls to 3 to 5 per cent of the Ah rating: on 100 Ah the charger drops to float as the topping current reaches 4 A, inside the drawn 3 to 5 A band

To cut the recharge time a battery may be recharged at 2.33 to 2.40 V a cell, and must switch to float when full: the 2.38 V boost reaches full before a charge at the float setting, then drops to 2.25 V
An equalising charge raises the voltage to 2.50 V a cell: the equalise stretch holds 2.50 V a cell, and 24 cells need 60.00 V
The gassing voltage is 2.40 V a cell: bubbles rise at 2.40 V a cell and above, never at the 2.38 V boost or on float
A charged, rested cell reads 2.1 V and the nominal voltage is 2 V a cell: 55 cells give 115.50 V and 110.00 V, both below the 122.65 V float setting

Full charge avoids sulfation on the negative plate, and over-saturation causes grid corrosion on the positive plate: below the float band only the sulphate meter rises, above it only the grid meter, and inside it neither
Recharge 1.2 times the discharged capacity: 50 Ah taken out needs 60 Ah put back, so about 83 per cent of the ampere-hours come back
Bulk holds 10 A while the volts per cell climb, topping holds the charge setting while the current falls, and float holds 2.25 V with a small current
51.60 V across 24 cells is 2.15 V a cell, below the float band, so a year there grows sulphate and no corrosion; boost at 2.40 V on 24 cells is 57.60 V
Each puzzle accepts only its right answer, and nothing in its picture gives the answer before Check
Fourteen screens: demonstrations and puzzles take turns, then three mixed puzzles end the lesson
Every demonstration settles within 4.6 s and ends where its screen says, every answer's motion settles within 2.5 s, and a spell of months takes 2 s

applied.problem: The worked example says the maker corrects only above 30 °C, but its manual also raises the float below 10 °C, and it contradicts the explanation; the rule is about cell temperature, not the room's.

Single-source figures are stated as universal: 3 to 5 per cent is one rule (BU), 2.33 to 2.40 V boost is one maker's, and 2.50 V equalise is one rule (the same maker equalises at 2.33 to 2.40 V); the gassing line lacked its citation [^4].
Screen 3's hint states the 3 to 5 per cent rule as a definition of full, and screen 5's hint says 110 V puts nothing in, which holds only for a charged battery, not a deeply discharged one.
A tyre does not hold its pressure for good once filled; it slowly loses some, which is why it is checked regularly, as the analogy itself says.

notes.problem: "Cells in a 12 V block" (6) cites source 11, whose quote is about primary and secondary cells and does not state six cells; research R47 (six 2 V cells make 12 V) supports it but is not in the lesson's sources.
Screen 13 and the equalise mark use 2.50 V a cell (BU); the cited maker equalises its vented cells at 2.33 to 2.40 V for up to 72 hours, so the right answer's 2.50 V is one rule, not every maker's.

The float band mixes one maker's 2.23 V at 20 °C with BU's 2.25 to 2.27 V at 25 °C, while the temperature slider applies BU's charge-voltage coefficient about 25 °C to the float; fine as a sketch, but the references differ.
